title: Rama's ring
hookLine: a ring with Rama's name, and why Hindus write that name a thousand times
carry: nama: the name carries the one it names

cards: Before the southern party leaves, Rama calls Hanuman aside. Of all the leaders and all the armies, it's Hanuman he picks out.

Sugriva's confidence in him is obvious, and Rama has his own reasons, going back to that first conversation on Rishyamuka, the sentence with not one word wrong. He takes something small off his finger and holds it out.
It's the kind of thing you'd give someone only if you were sure of them.

teach.b: It's a ring, engraved with Rama's name. Take this, Rama tells him, so that when you find her, she'll know you come from me, and won't be afraid. Hanuman will meet Sita as a stranger, a monkey in an enemy city.
Words alone might not be believed. A ring with his name will be. Why Hanuman?
Valmiki gives the reason: Sugriva is surest of him, and Rama sees his resolve. Hanuman takes the ring, raises it to his head with joined palms, and bows at Rama's feet. Then the month passes.
The parties to the east, west and north search everything and come back on time with nothing. Now everyone is waiting on the south. Notice what Rama sends: not a letter, his name.
In Hindu devotion that's no small detail. Nama, the divine name, is treated as carrying the one it names.
Nama japa, repeating God's name, is one of the most common Hindu practices: on a mala of beads, in a bhajan, under the breath on a bus.
Some devotees write it, filling notebooks page after page with Sri Rama, a practice called likhita japa, written repetition.

teach.h: THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.
teach.b: And many devotees say that wherever Rama's name is sung, Hanuman is there, listening. In the story, a name on a ring will tell Sita she isn't forgotten.
Many teachers read the chanting the same way: the name brings the one named close. That's how it meets a life now, in a grandmother's notebook, or Ram written at the top of a page.
And the week, in one line: from the rains to the ring, a friendship forgotten, warned, forgiven, and now carried in a name.

how: Nama japa, repeating a name of God, is among the most common Hindu practices, and many devotees write Rama's name in notebooks (likhita japa); in paintings and temple carvings, Hanuman is often shown kneeling before Sita and holding out Rama's ring.

o: a sealed letter Rama writes for Sita to read
a finger-ring, the token Rama gives Hanuman
a jewel Sita wears pinned high in her hair

games.q: the ring and the returns — tap the pairs.
p: the one Rama trusts with it

s: Rama gives the ring to Angada, the party's leader
the ring is meant to reassure Sita
so she'll know the messenger truly comes from Rama.
writing God's name over and over is a real Hindu practice
likhita japa: written repetition, often of Rama's name.

games.q: you're Rama. a stranger will have to win Sita's trust in an enemy city. what do you give him?
o: your ring, engraved with your name.
nothing: his words will be enough.
games.why: Rama sends his name on a ring: the name carries the one it names, so Sita knows he's near.

practice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God with the breath, sometimes on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Try it now: breathe in, and on the out-breath say Ram silently, or another name you love.
If you don't pray, use the name of someone who trusts you. When the mind wanders, let the name be the ring that brings you back.

wordCard.voice: Anguliya, a finger-ring: the one Rama gives Hanuman today, engraved with his name, so Sita will know he sent him.

orig.note: Sanskrit aṅgulīya: a finger-ring, from aṅguli, finger.

carryVoice: Your line: nama: the name carries the one it names. One small ring, one name, a lot of hope. Day five hundred ninety-five, done.
